entries.title: Mark 11:1
segments: He sendeth two of his disciples. It is not certain who they were; but the details given indicate an attentive eyewitness.  Most probably Peter, on whom Mark depended for his narrative, was one, and the other may have been James or John.

entries.title: Mark 11:10
segments: The kingdom of our father David. A proof that they were entirely ignorant, perhaps with the exception of a few, of the true character of the Messiah.  They still thought that Jesus intended to restore the earthly kingdom of David.

entries.title: Mark 11:11
segments:
He entered into Jerusalem. The city was thronged in the streets and on the housetops.  The scribes and Pharisees, and all the friends of the party of Herod and the Sadducees, must have fully realized at last the great power of Jesus over the multitude.  They must have feared deeply for the safety of the beliefs and institutions, which they championed.

entries.title: Mark 11:18
segments: All the multitude was astonished. They were on the verge of making a great public demonstration in his behalf.  This explains the fear of the chief priests and scribes.

entries.title: Mark 11:19
segments: Went forth out of the city. Showing his perfect fearlessness in the most imminent danger.

entries.title: Mark 11:20
segments: In the morning. On Tuesday, the day following the cleansing of the temple.

entries.title: Mark 11:23
segments: And shall not doubt in his heart. Whose faith shall remain steadfast and clear, even in the inmost recesses of the soul.  See

entries.title: Mark 11:24
segments: All things whatsoever ye pray and ask for, etc.  A-never-to-be-surpassed statement of the meaning of faith and prayer.  It is only the union of faith with prayer that produces results.  No petition made in doubt or despair can be answered.  Christ himself declares that in order that we may have or possess the things we ask for, we must first believe that God grants them.

entries.title: Mark 11:28
segments: By what authority doest thou these things? There is no record that Jesus was ever ordained as a rabbi.  If not, he had no official authority to teach, according to the requirements of Jewish custom.  It was his authority to call himself the Son of God and to do mighty works about which his enemies questioned him.  See notes on
